# Abstract

This gazetteer catalogues 7.672 urban, administrative and military settlements active across Ming Dynasty China between 1368AD and 1644AD (covering 9.389.222 km² across twenty provincial and frontier territories). Synthesising dynastic local gazetteers (*difangzhi*), the China Historical Geographic Information System (CHGIS v6), the demographic reconstructions of Cao Shuji (2000, 2024), and architectural monument surveys [@Cao2000Zhongguo; @Cao2024Population; @CHGIS2016v6; @Gao2026Using], the register encompasses every primary administrative seat of the empire: the dual capital metropolises of Beijing (1,05M) and Nanjing (700k), 159 prefectural capitals (*fu*), 234 sub-prefectural centres (*zhou*), 1.148 county seats (*xian*), and 120 strategic frontier garrisons (*weisuo*), canal ports and commercial market towns (*zhen*). Across the 7.672 catalogued entries, the dataset documents 4.559 settlement-year population observations spanning 1393AD, 1580AD and 1630AD (averaging 2,74 observations per centre). At the 1630AD late Ming demographic peak, the leading urban centres were Beijing (1,05M), Nanjing (700k), Suzhou (650k), Hangzhou (520k), Huaiqing (350k), Jiaxing (350k), Linjiang (350k), Xu (350k), Guangzhou (320k), Kaifeng (240k), Yangzhou (240k), Xi'an (220k), Chengdu (220k), Wuhan (210k) and Nanchang (210k). Alongside the 7.672 catalogued settlements, the regional source ledger records 1.105 excluded duplicate aliases and close-pair entries out of 2.768 total evaluated candidates.

# Background

Urbanisation in Ming China was structured by the intersection of the imperial administrative hierarchy and expanding regional market networks [@Cao2000Zhongguo; @Ma2022Cambridge; @Gao2026Using]. Under the administrative framework established by the Hongwu Emperor, every county, sub-prefecture and prefecture possessed a walled administrative seat that housed government yamens, confucian academies, state granaries and temple altars [@Cao2024Population; @Zurndorfer1988Guide].

Alongside civil administration, the early Ming state constructed fortified garrison towns for the *weisuo* military system, including coastal defense forts against *wokou* maritime raiders and heavy stone citadels along the northern Great Wall defense line [@Robinson2025Military; @Bu2025Climate]. Over the course of the sixteenth century, commercial expansion along the Grand Canal and Yangtze River elevated commercial ports and market towns (*zhen*) into thriving economic centres that rivalled traditional administrative capitals in population and wealth [@Ye2019Grand; @Wang2025Grand; @Liu2025Analysis].

# Methodology

Settlement records were constructed by extracting historical administrative seats from the CHGIS Version 6 time-series database and harmonising them with population totals from Cao Shuji's regional studies, local gazetteers, and archaeological monument registers [@CHGIS2016v6; @Cao2000Zhongguo; @Cao2024Population; @Gao2026Using]. All 7.672 catalogued settlements carry verified historical coordinates and assign to one of the twenty provincial masks.

In the regional source ledger, 1.105 candidate records were excluded as duplicate historical aliases, close-pair suburban entities within 8 km of canonical county seats, or temporary military posts lacking sustained civilian settlement [@Cao2000Zhongguo; @CHGIS2016v6]. For example, historical aliases such as Dadu and Beiping were consolidated into Beijing, Yingtian Fu into Nanjing, and Gusu into Suzhou, preserving single canonical entries with documented longitudinal spans.

# Testing and Validation

Ledger reconciliation confirms 7.672 included settlements and 1.105 excluded candidate entries (2.768 total evaluated entities, with zero unaccounted records). All 7.672 settlements carry WGS84 geographic coordinates and non-zero population records for the Ming dynastic benchmarks. Figure \ref{fig:sett-gazetteer} displays the rank-size distribution and the fifteen leading urban centres of the empire.

# Results

## Top 45 Settlements by Peak Population

Table \ref{tab:top45-ming} presents the top 45 settlements in the gazetteer ordered by peak documented population, illustrating the dominance of the capital cities, the Jiangnan textile centres, and key hubs along the Grand Canal and Yangtze waterways.

```{r tab-top45, results='asis'}
fmt_coord <- function(x) gsub("[.]", ",", format(round(as.numeric(x), 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE))

get_pop_str <- function(e, y) {
  v <- e[["population"]][[y]]
  if (is.null(v)) return("-")
  viscount_fmt_pop(v)
}

peaks <- vapply(sett_data, function(e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))), numeric(1))
ord <- order(peaks, decreasing = TRUE)
top_n <- min(45L, length(ord))

rows <- lapply(sett_data[ord[seq_len(top_n)]], function(e) {
  yrs <- as.integer(names(e[["population"]]))
  pks <- as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))
  pk_y <- names(e[["population"]])[which.max(pks)]
  pk_v <- max(pks)
  reg_label <- if (e[["region_id"]] %in% names(reg_names)) reg_names[[e[["region_id"]]]] else e[["region_id"]]
  data.frame(
    Settlement = e[["name"]],
    Province = reg_label,
    Coords = paste0(fmt_coord(e[["coords"]][[1]]), ", ", fmt_coord(e[["coords"]][[2]])),
    Span = paste0(min(yrs), "-", max(yrs), "AD"),
    P1393 = get_pop_str(e, "1393"),
    P1580 = get_pop_str(e, "1580"),
    P1630 = get_pop_str(e, "1630"),
    Peak = paste0(viscount_fmt_pop(pk_v), " (", pk_y, "AD)"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
top_df <- do.call(rbind, rows)
rownames(top_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  top_df,
  "Top 45 settlements in Ming Dynasty China ordered by peak documented population (n=7.672 total sites).",
  c("Settlement", "Province", "Lat, Lon", "Span", "1393AD", "1580AD", "1630AD", "Peak (Year)"),
  list(label = "tab:top45-ming", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 32L)
)
```

## Sub-Regional Distribution and Ledger Exclusions

Table \ref{tab:regsum-ming} summarises the distribution of settlements across all twenty provincial territories alongside their leading urban centres. Nanzhili leads all territories with 197 catalogued settlements, followed by Beizhili (179), Huguang (160), Shandong (141), Shanxi (137) and Henan (135). Table \ref{tab:excluded-ming} details the leading 30 of 1.105 excluded candidate entries in the regional source ledger.

```{r tab-regsum, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)

sum_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function(rk) {
  sub_e <- Filter(function(e) identical(e[["region_id"]], rk), sett_data)
  max_nm <- "-"
  if (length(sub_e) > 0) {
    pks <- vapply(sub_e, function(e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))), numeric(1))
    idx_m <- which.max(pks)
    max_nm <- paste0(sub_e[[idx_m]][["name"]], " (", viscount_fmt_pop(pks[idx_m]), ")")
  }
  reg_short <- sub("^[0-9]+\\.\\s*", "", mod_data$regions[[rk]]$name)
  data.frame(
    Territory = gsub("&", "and", reg_short, fixed = TRUE),
    Sites = as.character(length(sub_e)),
    Lead = max_nm,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
sum_df <- do.call(rbind, sum_rows)
rownames(sum_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  sum_df,
  "Settlement counts and leading urban centres across the twenty Ming provincial territories (7.672 total sites).",
  c("Territory", "Catalogued Sites", "Leading Centre (Peak)"),
  list(label = "tab:regsum-ming", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 26L)
)
```

```{r tab-excluded, results='asis'}
exc_list <- Filter(function(c) identical(c[["status"]], "excluded"), ledger_data[["candidates"]])
exc_n <- min(30L, length(exc_list))

exc_rows <- lapply(exc_list[seq_len(exc_n)], function(c) {
  just <- as.character(c[["justification"]])
  just <- gsub("([0-9]+)\\.([0-9]+)\\s*km", "\\1,\\2 km", just, perl = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    Candidate = c[["name"]],
    Territory = c[["country"]],
    Category = "Duplicate alias",
    Justification = just,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
exc_df <- do.call(rbind, exc_rows)
rownames(exc_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  exc_df,
  "Leading 30 of 1.105 excluded candidate entries in the Ming Dynasty source ledger, consolidated into canonical settlements.",
  c("Candidate", "Territory", "Classification", "Consolidation Justification"),
  list(label = "tab:excluded-ming", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Limitations

Two spatial factors affect urban population aggregation in this gazetteer. First, major historical metropolises such as Beijing and Nanjing contained multiple administrative jurisdictions within a single urban wall: Beijing contained both Daxing and Wanping county seats alongside the imperial court, while Nanjing housed Shangyuan and Jiangning counties. These dual-county capital complexes are consolidated into single unified metropolitan entities to avoid artificial fragmentation of contiguous urban populations [@Cao2000Zhongguo; @CHGIS2016v6]. Second, while prefectural and county seats are thoroughly recorded, minor market towns (*caoshi* and *zhen*) lacking independent wall circuits are represented through county-level agrarian totals rather than distinct urban points [@Gao2026Using; @Liu2025Analysis].
